title: Delete Node in a BST
description: Brute force to optimized: rebuilding a new BST from scratch versus in-place deletion using the in-order successor for the two-children case.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a BST and a key, delete the node with that value from the tree, and return the root of the resulting BST (which must remain a valid BST). If the key does not exist, return the tree unchanged.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Delete a node from a BST, keep it valid\"","Three distinct cases based on the node's number of children, with the hardest case (two children) resolved via the in-order successor"],["A node with two children needs a replacement that preserves BST ordering","The in-order successor (smallest value in the right subtree) is always a safe, order-preserving replacement"]]}

blocks.text: Deleting a node with no children or one child is straightforward: simply replace it with its (possibly null) child. Deleting a node with TWO children is trickier: replacing its value with its in-order successor (the smallest value in its right subtree) preserves BST ordering, and then that successor (which has at most one child, since it is the leftmost node in a subtree) can be removed from its original position using the simpler cases.

blocks.title: Analogy: Removing a Manager from an Org Chart Without Breaking Reporting Lines
blocks.text: Picture removing a manager from an org chart while keeping the reporting structure valid. If they have no or one direct report, that report (or nobody) simply takes their place. If they have two, the most natural replacement is the person who would come right after them in a specific ordering (their closest subordinate), promoted into their spot, with that subordinate's own original spot then filled in simply.

blocks.caption: Three cases: no children, one child (replace directly), two children (replace with in-order successor, then delete it)

blocks.text: Result (preorder): 5 4 2 null null null 6 null 7 null null. Node 3 has two children (2 and 4); its in-order successor is 4, which replaces it, and the original 4 is then removed.

Before rebuilding the tree from scratch, notice that deletion can be handled entirely in place: search for the node using BST ordering, then handle its removal based on how many children it has, using the in-order successor trick for the two-children case.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Standard BST search (comparing key to the current node, going left or right) locates the node to delete in O(height).

Observation 2: If the found node has no left child, its right child (possibly null) directly replaces it.

Observation 3: If it has no right child, its left child directly replaces it.

Observation 4: If it has BOTH children, its value is overwritten with its in-order successor's value (found by going right once, then left as far as possible), and that successor is then removed from its original position (which is guaranteed to have at most one child, since it is the leftmost node in its subtree, simplifying that removal to one of the earlier cases).
This leads to a recursive search-and-delete: find the node, then handle removal based on its children count, using the in-order successor for the two-children case.
Collect all values except the key via a traversal, then rebuild a brand new BST from scratch by inserting them one at a time.
Why the code is written this way

items: Rebuilding from scratch directly produces a valid BST without the key.
It discards the existing structure entirely, wasting nodes that could otherwise be reused.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case via naive insertion.
Space: O(n) for new nodes.
Limitation: in-place deletion, handling the three cases directly, avoids rebuilding the tree and any new node allocation for unaffected parts.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Search for the target node using BST ordering. Once found: no left child means replace with the right child; no right child means replace with the left child; both children present means overwrite the value with the in-order successor and recursively delete that successor from the right subtree (where it is guaranteed to have at most one child).
Recursively search for key; upon finding it, handle 0, 1, or 2 children as described, reattaching results as you unwind the recursion.

blocks.text: Replacing a two-children node's value with its in-order successor (the smallest value strictly greater than it) preserves BST ordering exactly, since the successor is guaranteed larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything remaining in the right subtree. Since the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, it has no left child, making its own removal simplify to the easy 0-or-1-child case.

blocks.text: Delete Node in a BST is the canonical BST deletion problem, requiring careful handling of the two-children case via the in-order successor.

items: Forgetting that the successor could have a right child that needs to be preserved when it is removed from its original spot.

blocks.text: Explaining the three cases clearly, especially why the in-order successor is a safe replacement preserving BST ordering, is essential to demonstrate full understanding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "delete from a BST, keep it valid", think: 0/1 child replace directly, 2 children swap with in-order successor then delete it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Rebuilding from scratch costs O(n squared) worst case; in-place deletion costs O(height) time and space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: in-place BST deletion, handling three cases by children count.
Core Idea: 0/1 child replaces directly; 2 children overwrite value with in-order successor, then delete the successor from its original spot.
Time: O(n squared) for rebuilding, O(height) for in-place deletion.
Space: O(n) new nodes versus O(height) extra.
Most Important Observation: the in-order successor always safely preserves BST ordering when replacing a two-children node.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, moderately hard BST manipulation problem.
One line memory trick: 0/1 child replace directly; 2 children swap with in-order successor, delete it.
